note: Each record is a verifiable, sourced incident. No synthetic entries. 'confidence' reflects strength of public documentation, not editorial judgement. Where a claim is contested, both the allegation and the response are recorded. v0.2 extends coverage through the 2025 WADA non-compliance episode and 2026 clearance.

records.title: Athletics Kenya diversion of Nike sponsorship funds
records.summary: IAAF Ethics Board found that senior Athletics Kenya officials diverted Nike 'honorarium' and service payments — including a USD 500,000 commitment bonus — into a 'Clearance Account' used for personal benefit rather than athlete support.
records.outcome: David Okeyo banned from track and field for life (2018). Officials denied wrongdoing, calling the contract 'executed with integrity'.

records.title: Rio 2016 chef de mission theft charges
records.summary: Kenya's Olympic team leader was charged over the theft of KES 25.6 million (~USD 256,000) meant for athletes' and officials' accommodation in Rio; two other officials were charged over misappropriated Nike-supplied team uniforms.
records.outcome: Charged; denied the charges. Team Kenya's Rio campaign, despite topping African medal counts, was widely described as beset by mismanagement.

records.title: Cabinet Secretary conviction over Rio 2016 preparation funds
records.summary: Kenya's former Sports Cabinet Secretary Hassan Wario was convicted for diverting KES 58 million in Rio Olympic preparation funds.
people_implicated: Hassan Wario Arero (Cabinet Secretary for Sports)
records.outcome: Convicted (2021); sentenced to six years, commuted to a KES 50 million fine.

records.title: WADA non-compliance and Rio eligibility crisis
records.summary: Kenya's national anti-doping organisation was declared non-compliant with the World Anti-Doping Code. The IOC ruled that Kenyan athletes' Rio eligibility be decided individually by each sport's international federation.
records.outcome: Kenya avoided a blanket ban; subsequently established the Anti-Doping Agency of Kenya (ADAK) and criminalised doping-related conduct.

records.title: Systemic doping among sub-elite and elite Kenyan distance runners
records.summary: The Athletics Integrity Unit characterises Kenya's problem as driven by a uniquely large 'pyramid' of professional-grade sub-elite runners for whom road-race prize money creates a doping market — distinct from state-sponsored models. More than 140-180 Kenyan athletes have been sanctioned since 2016.
people_implicated: Multiple athletes (e.g. Rhonex Kipruto, Ruth Chepngetich, Albert Korir — road/championship cases)
records.outcome: Kenyan government committed ~USD 5 million per year for five years to anti-doping; AIU began a five-year remediation plan; first lifetime ban issued 2024 (Beatrice Toroitich).
linked_medalists: Jemima Sumgong (2016 marathon gold; 2017 EPO ban, retained Olympic title)
Asbel Kiprop (2008 1500m gold; 2019 ban in separate case)

records.title: Killing of Agnes Tirop and the female-athlete exploitation pattern
records.summary: The murder of world-class runner Agnes Tirop (aged 25), with her husband named a key suspect, drew attention to financial exploitation and violence faced by Kenyan female athletes — who frequently serve as primary breadwinners for extended families while facing exploitation by coaches, agents and relatives.
records.outcome: National conversation on athlete welfare; contributed to later welfare-policy commitments. Handled here as a welfare/gender structural issue, not a true-crime item.

records.title: Olympic boycotts of 1976 and 1980
records.summary: Kenya did not compete at Montreal 1976 (African boycott over New Zealand's sporting ties to apartheid South Africa) or Moscow 1980 (US-led boycott), removing two Games from its medal record at the height of a strong distance-running generation.
records.outcome: Widely cited as costing Kenya an unknown number of likely medals (e.g. Henry Rono's era).

records.title: Nationality transfers of Kenyan-born runners
records.summary: A sustained pattern of Kenyan-born runners switching allegiance to Gulf states (Bahrain, Qatar) and others, driven by financial incentives and the depth of Kenyan competition. Some athletes later sought to reclaim Kenyan citizenship after negative experiences.
records.outcome: Ongoing policy and identity questions; documented in academic labour-migration literature.

records.title: Escalating AIU/ADAK sanction counts and the $25M WADA funding agreement
records.summary: Annual sanctions rose sharply: AIU suspended 28 Kenyan athletes in 2022, 25 in 2023, and 39 in 2024; ADAK suspended 34, 60, and 72 respectively over the same years. The AIU's ineligible list reached 119 Kenyan athletes by 31 December 2024, up from 54 two years earlier. Kenya signed a USD 25 million, five-year anti-doping funding agreement with WADA in 2022, though 2024 government budget cuts prompted President Ruto to personally pledge continued ADAK funding to IOC president Thomas Bach. ADAK's own budget subsequently rose roughly tenfold, from KES 20 million (FY2023/24) to KES 185 million (FY2024/25), alongside 4,161 tests conducted that year.
records.outcome: Testing volume and sanction counts both rose, reflecting increased enforcement capacity rather than a resolved problem; set up the 2025 WADA compliance crisis.

records.title: World Championship trials bans and the Chepngetich marathon world-record case
records.summary: Ahead of the 2025 World Athletics Championships in Tokyo, 20 Kenyan athletes were barred from national trials for missing mandatory out-of-competition tests under World Athletics Rule 15 (only 125 of 145 submitted athletes completed the first testing phase by the May 24 deadline). On 17 July, marathon world record holder Ruth Chepngetich was provisionally suspended after an out-of-competition sample (14 March) showed a concentration of 3,800 ng/ml against a WADA reporting threshold of 20 ng/ml.
people_implicated: Ruth Chepngetich (marathon world record holder, 2024 Chicago Marathon)
records.outcome: Chepngetich accepted a voluntary provisional suspension (19 April) ahead of the AIU's own provisional suspension; case outcome (standard two-year ban, subject to hearing) pending as of source publication.

records.title: WADA declares Kenya and ADAK non-compliant with the WADA Code
records.summary: Following a May 2024 audit under the International Standard for Code Compliance by Signatories (ISCCS), WADA's Executive Committee declared Kenya and ADAK non-compliant on 11 September 2025, with consequences (including loss of rights to host regional, continental, or world championships) set to take effect 3 October 2025 unless corrective action was taken or the finding disputed.
records.outcome: ADAK developed a corrective action plan addressing governance and oversight structures, operational independence, results management, and athlete whereabouts systems.

records.title: WADA clears Kenya from the non-compliance watchlist
records.summary: Following ADAK's corrective action plan, WADA expunged Kenya from its non-compliance watchlist, closing out the crisis opened in September 2025. Of 131 athletes tested by ADAK in the relevant window, 13% (18) were caught via out-of-competition testing and 86% (113) via in-competition testing; the AIU banned 19 individuals in 2025, down from 39 the prior year.
records.outcome: Kenya's hosting and competition rights were preserved; documented as a completed governance-response cycle from crisis (2025) to remediation (2026) — the clearest test case in this dataset for the governance-response scorecard methodology.
